1. What strange item permanently lives in your car?
Why it works: The object creates immediate curiosity, but the explanation supplies the real story.
JB & Sandy: “Why Is That in Your Car?” Callers reveal the object first—traffic cone, wedding dress, bowling ball, mannequin head—while JB and Sandy guess why it is there. Require photographic evidence for social.

items.title: How long do you go between washing sheets?
items.body: Sheets and towels should be every one to two weeks. A Sleep Advisor study says the average is about 24 days (25 for pillowcases). A UK study found most single men wait about four months, and 5% of people wash them once or twice a year. Phone: your honest number, and are the guest-room sheets a different story?
items.doc_text: Unknown Poll: Washing Sheets. It’s generally recommended that people wash their bedsheets and bath towels every one to two weeks, but as a study conducted by Sleep Advisor showed the average person pushed it to around 24 days (25 for pillowcases alone). Single men tend to be worse, as a UK study found, with a majority of them holding off on washing or changing bedsheets for four months. Think that’s gross? There are 5 percent of people overall who wash them once or twice…a year.

items.title: Your Optimus gets ONE chore forever
items.doc_text: What Job Would You Immediately Give to a Robot? Greg & The Morning Buzz discussed the increasing presence of robots Wednesday and asked which household jobs people would happily surrender—cleaning, litter boxes, snow removal, cooking. Amazon Music Austin twist: “Tesla gives you an Optimus tomorrow—but it can perform only ONE chore forever. What are you programming it to do?” Laundry? Yard? Dishes? H-E-B run? I think the interesting argument is whether you choose the most time-consuming chore or the one you simply hate most.

items.title: The job that looks awesome but sucks
items.doc_text: The Job Everyone Thinks Is Awesome—But Actually Sucks. Preston & Steve asked listeners Wednesday about overly romanticized jobs. Podscan Great topic if you require firsthand experience: “What job looks amazing from the outside but you’ve actually done it—and it’s terrible?” Bartender, flight attendant, radio personality, chef, realtor, teacher, musician, working on a boat. The rule: you must have actually held the job. That eliminates uninformed complaining.

items.title: What the next generation may not know how to do
items.doc_text: hat Are You Genuinely Worried the Next Generation Won’t Be Able to Do? Valentine also asked listeners about concerns for the next generation, including AI and shrinking attention spans. Sunny 105.3 Avoid the predictable “kids today” discussion. Ask: “What skill did everybody your age learn that you’re genuinely not sure your kids will ever need—or know how—to do?” Read a map, write cursive, drive a stick, use a paper dictionary, change a tire, memorize phone numbers, make change. Then younger listeners get to nominate skills JB & Sandy’s generation cannot do.

items.title: Empty Your Pockets
items.doc_text:
“What’s in Your Bag?”—But Turn It Into a Personality Test. Mojo in the Morning had people reveal what they carry around every day and the stories behind those items. Mojo in the Morning JB & Sandy could make this “Empty Your Pockets.” Without warning, every person in the studio empties pockets/purse/backpack onto the table. Pick the object that requires the most explanation. Then listeners text photos of theirs. Most inexplicable item wins. This is tailor-made for video.

items.doc_text: “What couple behavior makes you immediately suspicious?” Joint Facebook account? Shared email? Location tracking? Knowing each other’s passwords? One person answering the other’s phone? JB and Sandy rule each one Healthy / Weird / Something Happened Here. Then ask listeners with joint accounts to defend themselves.

items.title: Annual performance review
items.doc_text: Annual Performance Review.” Listeners submit one compliment and one complaint. Sandy serves as HR and presents them anonymously. Then reverse roles the next day. Save the best lines as imaging. This could generate both funny radio and extremely strong short video because the host has to react in real time.

items.title: The tiny household issue that became a marital dispute
items.doc_text: “What completely insignificant household issue has become a major marital dispute?” Throw pillows, thermostat, ceiling fan, dishwasher loading, decorative towels, number of pillows on the bed, where shoes belong. Ask every caller: “How many YEARS has this argument been going on?”

items.title: Is a birthday text enough?
items.doc_text: “Is a Birthday Text Enough?” “Who in your life still requires an actual PHONE CALL on their birthday?” Mom? Dad? Spouse? Sibling? Best friend? At what relationship level does a text become insulting? Then complicate it: Does a personalized video count more than a phone call? Does a Facebook ‘HBD!’ count at all? Great generational argument.

items.title: Tech you’d willingly downgrade
items.doc_text: “What piece of technology would you willingly downgrade?” Car without a touchscreen, dumb TV, flip phone, physical concert ticket, analog thermostat, actual key instead of an app. Then challenge a staff member to live with the old version for 48 hours.

items.title: The hobby that makes your spouse disappear
items.doc_text: “What hobby makes your spouse temporarily disappear?” Hunting season, fantasy football, golf, cycling, boating, gardening, gaming, Christmas decorating. Then ask: “How many hours a week before it officially becomes a second relationship?” That should generate great spouse-vs.-hobby calls.

items.title: The kid phrase that makes you reach for your wallet
items.doc_text: B & Sandy: “What phrase from your kid instantly makes you reach for your wallet?” “Dad, quick question…” “Hypothetically…” “Are you in a good mood?” “So everybody else is going…” Then flip it: What phrase did YOU use on your parents? Good multigenerational radio.

items.title: That’s where you lost me
items.doc_text: “That’s Where You Lost Me.” What tiny thing immediately makes you bail? Restaurant has a 90-minute wait? I’m out. Party requires a costume? I’m out. Concert has no seats? I’m out. Vacation involves sharing a bathroom? I’m out. Let callers finish one sentence: “I was interested until you said _____.”

items.title: Open houses with zero intention of buying
items.doc_text: “Have you ever gone to an open house with absolutely ZERO intention of buying?” Why? Nosy about neighbor’s house, wanted to see inside an expensive home, free cookies, checking out an ex’s neighborhood. Then: “What did you discover inside someone’s house that surprised you?”

items.title: What did someone finally talk you into trying?
items.doc_text: “What did somebody finally talk you into trying—and were they right?” Pickleball, Pilates, sushi, audiobook, cold plunge, TikTok, Costco, cruise, electric bike. Then JB and Sandy each have to nominate one thing the other must try before Friday. Now the topic produces future content.

items.title: The closest you’ve come to getting arrested
items.doc_text: “Which Cast Members Got Arrested!?” and a Worst Date Ever involving an arrest. Don’t copy the benchmark—use the broader question: “What is the closest you have ever come to getting arrested?” College prank, public intoxication scare, mistaken identity, traffic incident, dumb youthful decision. Keep it to nonviolent/minor stories and the calls should be fantastic.

items.title: The hobby that suddenly got cool again
items.doc_text: Mahjong Is Suddenly Everywhere—Use the Hobby Nobody Expected to Become Cool., while current mahjong leagues/classes around the country are selling out or expanding. The radio topic is: “What hobby suddenly became cool again?” Mahjong, pickleball, knitting, vinyl, film cameras, gardening, birding. Austin twist: make JB and Sandy each learn one “unexpectedly hot” hobby for a week and report back.

items.title: What dead Austin business would you bring back?
items.doc_text: “What store would you bring back tomorrow if you could?” Blockbuster, Tower Records, Toys “R” Us in its old form, Circuit City, Foley’s, old mall stores. Then localize it: “What dead Austin business would you resurrect?” That second hour could be excellent for heritage listeners.What Dead Austin Business Would You Bring Back? This feels strongest for immediate phones because it uses JB & Sandy’s history in the city and gives listeners a nostalgia lane syndicated shows can’t duplicate.

items.title: The struggle meal you didn’t know was a struggle meal
items.doc_text: “What meal did your family eat because it was cheap that you didn’t realize was a ‘struggle meal’ until you were older?” Buttered noodles, beans and rice, breakfast for dinner, canned chili, hot dogs cut into macaroni. Then ask: “Do you STILL love it?” That second question brings nostalgia rather than embarrassment.
